channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - All Critical Infrastructure
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] Boston Scientific clears most of the shipping backlog at day twelve — and no controller was ever touched
item.description: Boston Scientific is now nearly two weeks into recovery from the 25 August intrusion, and the shape of the damage is settled: an IT-side compromise that stopped a manufacturer anyway. Shipping has been restored for the majority of products at major distribution centres globally, with customer orders progressively clearing a backlog the company says will take time to work through. Manufacturing remains the slower half and no restoration date has been given. Working with CrowdStrike and other third parties, the company reports growing confidence that the access was confined to select internal-facing IT infrastructure, with no malicious activity since 25 August and implanted device function unaffected. No entry route, vulnerability or ransomware claim has been named. For OT defenders the absence is the point: nothing reached a PLC, yet losing the systems that tell a plant what to build and where to ship it has now cost twelve days. - Boston Scientific incident page and SEC filing, plus SecurityWeek and Industrial Cyber recovery reporting — also covered by MedTech Dive, Supply Chain Dive, TechCrunch and CBS News - Detected 25 Aug 2026; disclosed 26 Aug 2026; manufacturing disruption confirmed 28 Aug 2026; company updates 30 Aug 2026 and 4 Sep 2026, the latter confirming majority shipping restoration at major distribution centres — re-verified 6 Sep 2026, 6:16 PM ET

item.title: [Critical] The water campaign, quantified: CISA counts 100-plus internet-exposed systems hit, with controller logic and alarms altered
item.category: Incident — Confirmed OT disruption, water sector; CISA-quantified scale
item.description: CISA has put a figure on July’s campaign against US water utilities: malicious activity against more than 100 internet-exposed systems in the Water and Wastewater Systems sector, commonly programmable logic controllers wired straight into a cellular modem. The FBI records incidents at utilities in at least seven states since 27 July, with reporting placing targeting across at least a dozen. Some degraded operations — lost pressure, flooding, plants run by hand — though supply was not widely interrupted, and in several intrusions actors altered controllers to disable shutdown processes and alarms, letting unsafe conditions develop unannounced. US officials assess Iranian actors as likely responsible and describe the activity as largely opportunistic. It stays on the page five weeks on because of the admission behind the number: the exposure that carried it was in nobody’s asset register. - CISA exposure-reduction guidance and the FBI/EPA public service announcement — corroborated by SecurityWeek, Cybersecurity Dive, TechCrunch and The Register; Minnesota impact detail from state officials and SecurityWeek - Scale confirmed and reported 26 Aug 2026; observed activity July 2026; FBI PSA issued 30 Jul 2026 — re-verified 6 Sep 2026, 12:17 PM ET

item.title: [High] The water campaign was not the whole campaign — telecoms and energy control systems are now being probed, and there is a $10 million bounty on the man said to run it
item.category: Targeting — Iran-linked campaign widens beyond water into telecommunications and energy; attempts reported, no confirmed OT impact
item.description: Two developments this week moved the summer’s dominant OT story past the water sector. NBC News reported on 2 September, citing four people with access to government and industry threat information, that Iran-linked operators have spent recent weeks probing internet-facing automated control systems at telecommunications and energy providers as well as water utilities — and that those attempts have so far been unsuccessful. A day later the State Department’s Rewards for Justice programme posted a reward of up to $10 million for information identifying or locating Amir Yaryab, named as head of the cyber operations division of the IRGC Cyber-Electronic Command and accused of directing groups including the CyberAv3ngers persona against US critical infrastructure. Separately, a Telegram channel presenting itself as a voice for Iranian cyber operations has threatened action against US energy, water and telecommunications, without evidence of any successful operation. The signal for defenders is the change of aim, not a new capability: the same tradecraft that found exposed water PLCs in July is now being pointed at neighbouring sectors that run the same internet-facing gear. - NBC News reporting on expanded targeting and the State Department Rewards for Justice announcement, as carried by The Record — water-campaign scale from CISA and SecurityWeek - NBC report 2 Sep 2026; $10 million reward announced 3 Sep 2026 — verified 6 Sep 2026, 12:17 PM ET

item.title: [Critical] Attackers walked from a wind farm’s firewall to another plant’s PLCs across a shared cellular APN — and stopped a turbine
item.category: Incident — Confirmed OT disruption, energy; first documented private-APN pivot
item.description: CERT Polska’s follow-up report on attacks against Poland’s energy sector documents an intrusion path that maps almost exactly onto the exposure CISA and the NCSC are now warning about, and it is the reason this older item belongs on the page. Attackers compromised a FortiGate firewall at a wind farm, moved to a Teltonika cellular router, and then crossed a private cellular APN that had been provisioned without client isolation — meaning every SIM on that APN could reach every other. On the far side sat a WAGO PFC200 at a separate combined heat and power plant, still carrying default administrator credentials, which the attackers used to build an SSH bridge into the OT network. From there they forced three Siemens PLCs into STOP and set password protection on them, shutting down a steam turbine and the process-water treatment serving a town of roughly 50,000 people. CERT Polska assesses this as the first documented real-world OT intrusion via lateral movement across a private APN, and notes the shared-APN-without-isolation configuration is common in Poland and likely well beyond it. - CERT Polska energy-sector incident follow-up report, as reported by BleepingComputer — corroborated by SecurityWeek - Report published 10 Aug 2026; underlying incident occurred 2025 — verified 6 Sep 2026, 12:17 PM ET

item.title: [Critical] A small UK generating station ran manually for four days after an Iran-linked cyberattack
item.category: Incident — Confirmed OT disruption, power generation (UK)
item.description: A small British power generating station was taken offline for four days by a cyberattack, with staff forced to restore operations manually. The Telegraph broke the story on 22 August; the UK government confirmed that a small-scale generator had been affected while stating there was at no point a risk to the national energy system, and the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero has since contacted power companies about the risk. UK assessments reported by the Telegraph point to hackers affiliated with the Iranian regime, likely the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The site’s size is the uncomfortable part rather than a reassurance: distributed generation, embedded generators and behind-the-meter assets sit below most reporting thresholds, are often remotely operated by a third party, and are numerous enough that an attack that works once is repeatable. - SecurityWeek and CNBC, both citing the originating Telegraph report and the UK government statement - Incident occurred July 2026; reported 22–23 Aug 2026; government response reported 24 Aug 2026 — re-verified 6 Sep 2026, 12:17 PM ET

item.title: [High] Washington has put a name and a $10 million price on the officer who runs CyberAv3ngers
item.category: Incident — Nation-state attribution; the command behind the water, energy and telecom targeting is named
item.description: The State Department’s Rewards for Justice programme posted a $10 million reward on 3 September for information on Amir Yaryab, identified as the head of the IRGC’s Cyber-Electronic Command. The listing states that Yaryab directs operations against critical-infrastructure sectors including defence, shipping, energy, telecommunications and finance across the United States, Europe and the Middle East, and that he oversees the IRGC-CEC-affiliated groups CyberAv3ngers, Dadeh Afzar Arman and Mehrsam Andisheh Saz Nik, plus the Shahid Hemmat and Shahid Shushtari units. For OT defenders the significance is organisational rather than technical: CyberAv3ngers is the crew behind the Unitronics PLC defacements of 2023–24 and is the same lineage US agencies have tied to this summer’s campaign against internet-exposed water systems in at least twelve states. The reward confirms that the water, energy and telecom activity being tracked separately reports up through a single military command with a standing mission against civilian infrastructure — which is a statement about persistence, not about any new capability. Nothing in the listing suggests the tempo will fall; a named commander is a diplomatic and law-enforcement lever, not a mitigation. - US State Department Rewards for Justice listing — corroborated by The Record and multiple international outlets; underlying OT activity documented by CISA and the FBI - Reward announced 3 Sep 2026; reported 4 Sep 2026 — verified 6 Sep 2026, 10:30 PM ET

item.title: [Critical] Five agencies say the S7 family is being actively hunted — and that the exploit scripts are being written with AI
item.category: NSA/CISA/FBI/DOE/EPA joint advisory AA26-231A — active targeting of Siemens S7 series PLCs
item.description: The joint advisory published on 19 August is the primary-source anchor under this edition’s AI research. The NSA, CISA, FBI, DOE and EPA report threat actors actively working against Siemens S7 controllers that are internet-exposed or poorly segmented, spanning the S7‑200, ‑300, ‑400, ‑1200 and ‑1500 lines, and name Critical Manufacturing, Energy, Water and Wastewater, Chemical, Food and Agriculture and Commercial Facilities as the most affected sectors. What makes it notable is the method: the agencies describe AI‑generated reconnaissance and exploitation scripts built around the open-source python‑snap7 library and disguised to look like legitimate OT monitoring tooling. Two familiar conditions do the enabling — internet exposure through weak segmentation, and default or weak credentials. The protocol expertise that used to gate ICS exploit development is no longer the barrier. - CISA joint advisory AA26-231A (NSA, CISA, FBI, DOE, EPA) — corroborated by SecurityWeek, Tenable and Infosecurity Magazine - Published 19 Aug 2026 — re-verified 6 Sep 2026, 12:17 PM ET

item.title: [High] Eighteen frontier models were run at a real enterprise network. One completed the whole kill chain unaided.
item.category: Booz Allen Cyber Weapon Index — measured offensive capability of frontier AI models
item.description: Booz Allen published its Cyber Weapon Index on 4 September, testing eighteen US and Chinese frontier AI models against a production-grade enterprise network. One — Anthropic’s Claude Mythos — autonomously executed a full cyber kill chain, both starting from a stolen employee credential and, in the harder run, with no credentials at all. Roughly two-thirds of the models tested reliably gained initial access to a defended network without credentials, and the firm expects most to reach full autonomous kill-chain capability within about six months. The finding defenders should hold onto is the one the headline buries: every frontier API model scored zero against real, previously unknown vulnerabilities. Strong performance came against flaws deliberately introduced for the test. Booz Allen also reports that the “attack harness” — the tooling, memory and autonomy wrapped around a model — matters as much as the model, so cheap engineering can lift a weaker model close to frontier performance. None of the testing was OT-specific. - Booz Allen Cyber Weapon Index / The Offensive Frontier: AI as the Attacker, via Industrial Cyber - Published 4 Sep 2026 — verified 6 Sep 2026, 12:17 PM ET

item.title: [High] A frontier model ported a working PLC exploit to a second controller in eight hours — then bricked it
item.category: Forescout Vedere Labs — AI-assisted exploit development against PLCs
item.description: Forescout’s Vedere Labs published the result of a deliberately awkward experiment: point a frontier AI model at real industrial hardware and see how far it gets. Starting from the team’s own remote code execution exploit for a WAGO 750-852, built on CVE-2021-31886 — a pre-authentication overflow in the Nucleus FTP server — they asked Claude to port it to the related 750-831, giving the model a terminal, Ghidra and the physical device. It worked, but not cleanly. The first model tried failed to trace the vulnerable function; a stronger model eventually worked out why the injected shellcode was being wiped before it could run, and once past that it produced two working payloads in twelve minutes. Total cost of the final stage: over eight hours and more than $500 in API charges. A follow-up attempt at a command-and-control implant wrote to flash and permanently bricked the PLC. - Forescout Research – Vedere Labs report, via SecurityWeek — corroborated by Cybersecurity Dive with direct comment from Vedere Labs - Published 1 Sep 2026; corroborating reporting 1–2 Sep 2026 — verified 6 Sep 2026, 12:17 PM ET

item.title: [High] The router became the implant: a China-nexus crew lived inside Cisco IOS XR and switched off the logs that would have shown it
item.category: Threat intel — China-nexus espionage on carrier-grade routing; critical-infrastructure networks probed
item.description: Sygnia has published an account of an espionage campaign it tracks as Fire Ant operating inside Cisco IOS XR routers — not as a stepping stone to a server, but as the collection platform itself. The actor captured traffic passing through the devices while suppressing the evidence of its own presence, then moved on to the TACACS+ authentication infrastructure and Linux management hosts that sit behind them, harvesting the credentials that administer the rest of the estate. From that position it probed networks associated with critical infrastructure. Sygnia is careful about what it did and did not see: activity against those critical-infrastructure networks was scanning and connection attempts, not established compromise. It assesses strong overlap with operations publicly attributed to the China-nexus cluster UNC3886 without treating the two as the same thing. - Sygnia research, reported by Cybersecurity Dive — also carried by CSO Online, Network World and The Hacker News - Research published and reported early Sep 2026 — re-verified 6 Sep 2026, 12:17 PM ET

item.title: [Critical] CERT Polska confirms attackers are taking full control of internet-facing MikroTik routers — the box that quietly backhauls half the remote sites in your fleet
item.category: MikroTik RouterOS — “MikroTrick” pre-auth SSH takeover chain, confirmed exploited since 2 Sep
item.description: CERT Polska disclosed six RouterOS vulnerabilities on 5 September and confirmed that two of them are already being chained in live attacks. The chain, named MikroTrick, pairs CVE-2026-67276 (CVSS 9.2) — RouterOS validated only part of an SSH RSA public key, so an attacker who knows a username and the key’s public modulus can forge a key and log in without the private half — with CVE-2026-86060 (CVSS 9.2), a username-parsing flaw that hands the resulting session full administrative rights. Together they give unauthenticated device takeover wherever SSH answers from the internet. A third flaw, CVE-2026-67277 (CVSS 8.8), leaks kernel memory or reboots the device through the unauthenticated bandwidth-test service. MikroTik patched on 3 September in 6.49.21, 7.23.4, 7.24.2 and 7.25beta3. CERT Polska says confirmed compromises trace to 82.192.72.4 and run back to at least 2 September. This matters in OT because RouterOS is the cheap, ubiquitous router behind remote pump stations, substations, wellheads, irrigation skids and contractor-built field cabinets — equipment that is frequently outside the OT asset register and reachable from the internet by design. - CERT Polska (CSIRT NASK) warning and its companion CVE page, with MikroTik’s September 2026 security bulletin — corroborated by The Hacker News and Security Affairs - Patches released 3 Sep 2026; CERT Polska exploitation warning published 5 Sep 2026; attacks observed since at least 2 Sep 2026 — verified 7 Sep 2026, 12:20 AM ET

item.title: [Critical] CISA put SonicWall’s exploited SMA1000 pair in KEV a day after disclosure — a CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw chained to code execution
item.category: SonicWall SMA1000 — Two zero-days exploited, CVSS 10 chain, now in CISA KEV
item.description: SonicWall disclosed on 1 September that two previously unknown vulnerabilities in its SMA1000 secure remote access gateway and SSL-VPN appliance have been exploited in the wild, and CISA added both to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 2 September as part of a seven-CVE batch. CVE-2026-83548, carrying a CVSS score of 10, is a pre-authentication server-side request forgery in the Appliance Work Place interface that lets an unauthenticated attacker reach sensitive functionality; CVE-2026-83549, at 7.8, is an OS command injection flaw in the Appliance Management Console that an authenticated attacker can turn into remote code execution. SonicWall says it observed exploitation of both, which points to the pair being chained for unauthenticated code execution on the appliance. The vendor found the flaws and the attacks internally, and has published no indicators of compromise. Models 6210, 7210 and 8200v are affected. For OT operators this is the exact class of device that vendor engineers, integrators and on-call staff use to reach the plant from outside — a box that sits at the boundary, terminates trusted sessions and is rarely covered by an OT change window. - SonicWall PSIRT advisory SNWLID-2026-0016 and the CISA KEV addition of 2 Sep 2026 — reported by SecurityWeek and Help Net Security - Advisory published 1 Sep 2026; added to CISA KEV 2 Sep 2026 — verified 6 Sep 2026, 12:17 PM ET

item.title: [High] CISA’s 3 September batch lands on the remote-access client itself — a CVSS 9.6 root-level flaw in IXON VPN
item.category: CISA ICS advisory batch — ICSA-26-246 series; industrial remote access, SCADA platform, engineering tooling
item.description: The five advisories CISA published on 3 September are worth reading in a particular order, because the first one sits on the exact attack path two national agencies spent last week warning about. ICSA-26-246-02 covers CVE-2026-75925 in the IXON VPN Client below 1.4.7, rated CVSS v3.1 9.6: the client’s local configuration interface accepts changes without authenticating the requester, and does not neutralise line-ending sequences before writing them to a file that a privileged subprocess later consumes — so an attacker can inject extra directives and have commands run as root or SYSTEM. The injected configuration survives reboots, and the VPN keeps working normally, so nothing about the machine’s behaviour tells the engineer using it that anything changed. This is the software sitting on maintenance laptops and engineering workstations that reach machines in the field. The rest of the batch is more routine but not trivial: ICSA-26-246-06 flags CVE-2026-77393 in Inductive Automation Ignition 8.1.53 and earlier at CVSS 8.8, where the Gateway’s Create Project Role(s) setting shipped blank and any authenticated user able to run gateway scripts can create projects; ICSA-26-246-03 covers CVE-2026-12663 in Rockwell ControlFLASH 15.07 and earlier, whose installer granted the Everyone group write access to a product directory; ICSA-26-246-01 covers CVE-2026-77477 in the OPC Foundation UA LocalDiscoveryServer installers; and ICSA-26-246-08 covers a missing-authorization issue, CVE-2026-82684, in Tycon Systems TPDIN-Monitor-WEB3 2.2.9 and earlier that could expose credentials, configuration or flash contents. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-246-01, -02, -03, -06 and -08 — summarised by the Viakoo/Security Boulevard daily OT briefing; IXON technical detail cross-checked against the vendor security advisory page and CVE records - Advisories published 3 Sep 2026 — verified 6 Sep 2026, 12:17 PM ET

item.title: [High] CISA’s 1 September batch is five-sixths Rockwell — and it reaches the Logix controllers themselves
item.category: ICSA-26-244-01 to -05 + Rockwell PSIRT — a dozen-plus fixes, controllers included
item.description: CISA published eight ICS advisories on 1 September, and five of them are Rockwell Automation. The set covers RSLinx Classic (ICSA-26-244-01), the Redundancy Module Configuration Tool (-02), the Logix platform (-03), FactoryTalk Activation Manager (-04) and the ControlLogix, CompactLogix, CompactLogix 5480, GuardLogix and Compact GuardLogix controller families (-05). The RSLinx item is the one most sites will feel first: four flaws — CVE-2026-9621, CVE-2026-9622, CVE-2026-9624 and CVE-2026-9625 — let crafted Common Industrial Protocol traffic crash the communications service on version 4.50 and earlier, and it stays down until somebody restarts it by hand. RSLinx is the data path between controllers and the HMI, historian and engineering workstations, so a crash there is a visibility outage on a running process, not an IT inconvenience. The batch also carries an update to the Rockwell 1734 POINT I/O advisory (ICSA-26-202-09, Update A) and Update G to the long-running Mitsubishi Electric FA engineering software advisory (ICSA-24-135-04). Rockwell’s own round-up, reported 2 September, puts the total above a dozen fixes and adds detail the CISA summaries do not: remote code execution in FactoryTalk Historian, privilege escalation in FactoryTalk Activation Manager and in the Redundancy Module Configuration Tool, arbitrary code execution through the ControlFLASH firmware utility, cross-site scripting plus a web-server denial of service in ArmorStart distributed motor controllers, and further denial-of-service issues in 1756-ENBT and in Logix controllers via a third-party component. One item needs care rather than alarm: Rockwell’s advisory for CVE-2026-9637, a high-severity denial of service in ControlLogix and CompactLogix, is flagged as exploited in its document header but listed as not exploited in the body, and CISA states it is not aware of exploitation — read it as a documentation inconsistency, not a live campaign, and patch it on its merits. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-244-01 through -05 published 1 Sep 2026, plus ICSA-26-202-09 Update A and ICSA-24-135-04 Update G, read against the Rockwell Automation security advisory index and SecurityWeek’s 2 Sep 2026 round-up of the full Rockwell set - Published 1 Sep 2026 — verified 6 Sep 2026, 12:17 PM ET

item.title: [Medium] The free assessment most small utilities actually used is being withdrawn — and nothing at that price replaces it
item.category: Policy — CISA ends six free critical-infrastructure assessments; direct impact on small utilities and municipal operators
item.description: CISA is stopping six of the free cybersecurity assessments it has offered critical-infrastructure operators, according to reporting on an internal 25 August meeting in which the acting head of the agency’s Integrated Operations Division told staff to cease performing them. All six were regional-adviser engagements — an adviser sits with an operator, works through structured questions using the agency’s Cyber Security Evaluation Tool, and produces a report of prioritised improvements — and they covered intrusion detection and containment, ransomware readiness and supply-chain risk. The change follows the loss of roughly a third of CISA’s workforce. The operators affected are the ones with the least capacity to absorb it: small water systems, rural electric co-ops, municipal transit and county government, for whom a free structured assessment was often the only external review they would ever get. Commercial equivalents exist; they are not priced for a utility serving four thousand people. - Cybersecurity Dive reporting, carried by Utility Dive — based on an internal CISA meeting; no formal agency notice published as of this edition - Direction given 25 Aug 2026; reported 3 Sep 2026 — verified 6 Sep 2026, 12:17 PM ET

item.title: [Medium] Britain moves to take the power to disconnect your suppliers — and a four-day generator outage is what tabled the amendment
item.category: UK Cyber Security and Resilience Bill — Supplier designation powers, UK
item.description: Late amendments to the UK Cyber Security and Resilience Bill would give ministers power to stop critical-sector organisations using technology suppliers judged high risk. The Bill was introduced in November 2025, has cleared the Commons and sits in the Lords as HL Bill 32, close to Royal Assent; the amendments were tabled on 24 August, two days after reporting that Iran-linked actors had forced a small UK generating site offline for four days (see Incidents & Attacks). The approach is a departure worth noting: rather than only demanding better in-house security from operators, it lets government cut them off from third parties it considers inadequately secured, regardless of the supplier’s size or sector. The Bill already carries strict incident-reporting timelines and heavy penalties. Practitioners quoted in the coverage make the obvious point — a small integrator or managed service provider with standing remote access into a plant may not think of itself as critical national infrastructure, but a designation regime will decide that for it. - SecurityWeek reporting on the tabled amendments, read against the UK government’s Cyber Security and Resilience Bill collection on gov.uk - Amendments tabled 24 Aug 2026; reported 2 Sep 2026; Bill awaiting Royal Assent — verified 6 Sep 2026, 12:17 PM ET

item.title: [Medium] In one week, anyone selling a connected product into the EU owes a 24-hour warning on exploited vulnerabilities
item.category: EU Cyber Resilience Act — Reporting obligations effective 11 Sep 2026
item.description: The EU Cyber Resilience Act enters its reporting phase on 11 September 2026. From that date, manufacturers of products with digital elements must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe security incidents affecting their products, with an early warning inside 24 hours and a fuller notification inside 72 hours. The scope reaches far past consumer IoT: PLCs, RTUs, drives, gateways, HMIs, protocol converters and the engineering software around them are products with digital elements, and the obligation follows the manufacturer regardless of where the affected device is installed. Legal analysts advise naming an owner now and building the assessment, escalation and customer-communication path in advance, coordinating it with existing NIS2 and GDPR duties rather than standing up a third parallel process. - Freshfields analysis via Lexology, surfaced in the Viakoo/Security Boulevard daily OT briefing - Analysis published 1 Sep 2026; obligations effective 11 Sep 2026 (forward-looking) — verified 6 Sep 2026, 12:17 PM ET

item.title: [Info] The federal answer to the water campaign is a six-month, no-cost red-team pilot — and Texas is the test bed
item.category: Policy — US water sector; federal/state pilot offering free OT assessment and monitoring to utilities
item.description: Project Watershed 250 was launched in San Antonio on 31 August by the Office of the National Cyber Director and Texas Cyber Command, with the EPA and CISA as federal partners and the Texas governor’s office coordinating utility participation. It is a six-month pilot: participating water and wastewater systems get red-team stress testing of their networks, asset visibility and continuous monitoring, vulnerability prioritisation and segmentation help, at no cost to the utility. Vendors named in the rollout include Dragos, Forescout, Fortinet, Tenable, Palo Alto Networks and several hyperscalers; Forescout confirmed its participation and the specific services on 4 September. The administration has said it intends to extend the model nationally if the pilot works. The programme predates this summer’s intrusions but lands directly on the exposure they revealed — small systems with no security staff and remote-access paths nobody owns. - Office of the Texas Governor / ONCD, reported by Nextgov/FCW; Forescout release - Launched 31 Aug 2026 — partner services detailed 4 Sep 2026
